title: Toward unity
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox continue dialogue and marked 1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025

cards: Two old men in long robes walk toward each other in Jerusalem. One is the bishop of Rome, the other the patriarch of Constantinople.
Their churches have been divided a long time, with excommunications on the books, hurt on both sides, and a long habit of not speaking. They don't sign a treaty or settle a single doctrine.
They embrace, and exchange a kiss of peace, the way the liturgy does it. A small gesture. Afterward, the old excommunications are lifted, and the two churches begin talking in earnest.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: At the supper before his arrest, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims, "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee."
The Catholic Church takes that prayer as a task, not a wish.
Catholics and Orthodox already share a great deal: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, the Creed of Nicaea, the early councils, the Mother of God, the saints, the icons.
They have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together, remembering a creed they both still pray.
What divides them is real too, above all the role of the bishop of Rome, and it is worked on slowly, in official dialogue, by theologians from both sides.
Then the honest part. Eastern Catholic churches speak of themselves as a sign that East and West can share one communion. Some Orthodox see them differently, as a wound from the past.
Catholic and Orthodox theologians have said together that bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today.
Both views are held by people of good faith. Last, what's in reach now.

teach.h: ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM.
teach.b: Paul writes, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." Catholics and Orthodox can pray for each other, visit each other, learn each other's hymns, and greet each other at Pascha with the same words.
The day of full communion isn't here. But the embrace came first, before any agreement, and the road starts there.

how: The Catholic Church takes part in official theological dialogue with the Orthodox churches, and popes and patriarchs meet, pray together and exchange delegations on their churches' patronal feasts; Catholics pray for Christian unity, including during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

games.q: you're the bishop of Rome, meeting the patriarch of Constantinople after a long division, with nothing yet agreed. what do you do?
o: insist on a signed agreement first.
embrace him and exchange a kiss of peace.
keep the meeting to a formal handshake.

practice: On the in-breath, picture a Latin church you know: the altar, the pews, the crucifix.

On the out-breath, picture one of the Eastern churches from these days, a wall of icons, a priest's family, a cedar, a candle passed hand to hand, and keep breathing between the two, letting neither crowd out the other.
If you pray, pray Jesus's own words, that they all may be one; if you don't, hold both pictures side by side, at peace.

wordCard.voice: Toward unity. The long work of Catholics and Orthodox to become one communion again, through prayer, dialogue and friendship, begun with an embrace. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one day together. Tomorrow a new stretch begins: devotions. That's today, done.
